metadata.note: The lesson names no assigned reading on its visible slides. Reading questions rest on documents the lesson cites and quotes (Tron developer documentation on the resource model and consensus, the USDT contract on Tron, Fabric documentation on the ordering service and private data, Ongaro on Raft, Castro and Liskov on PBFT, Androulaki et al.), and each states a fact that is on a visible slide. Only the visible slides count; the hidden slides (Scenario onward) get no questions. Coverage: one question for each visible check (q4, q9, q11), worked (q5, q6), practice (q14), answers (q15) and review (q16) slide; q21 (Raft) and q22 (PBFT) cover the consensus bullets of the permissioned slide.

questions.question_stem: An analyst who has read Ethereum transfers on day 3 opens a USDT transfer on Tron. Which skill carries over?
questions.correct_answer: Reading it as on Ethereum: same key and 20 bytes, and a USDT transfer is a TRC-20 contract call that logs a Transfer.
incorrect_answers: Reading it as on Bitcoin: coins are spent from earlier outputs, and a USDT transfer is a new output script now.
Reading it as on a permissioned ledger: the operator keeps the records and shows a USDT transfer only to members.
None of it, since Tron has its own account and token design and a USDT transfer there needs a separate reading method.
questions.explanation: Tron reads like Ethereum: the same key and 20 bytes make the address, and TRC-20 matches ERC-20, so a USDT transfer emits a Transfer log as on day 3. What is new is who produces the blocks and who pays the Energy.
questions.lesson_block: What carries over: T-addresses and 19 of 27
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/permissioned_ledger/01-PC-permissioned_distributed_ledgers.qmd: What carries over: T-addresses and 19 of 27

questions.question_stem: Why does a US analyst on a stablecoin case need to know Tron, and not Ethereum alone?
questions.correct_answer: As of 31 Oct 2026 Tron held over half of USDT, and stablecoins carry most illicit volume, so cases often run through it.
incorrect_answers: Tron is the only chain where Tether can freeze USDT, so every freeze in a case has to be read from Tron alone.
Tron's Super Representatives can name the owner of any address, so a trace on that chain always ends at a named person there.
Ethereum holds almost no USDT at present, so a USDT case seldom needs the chain that day 3 taught the analyst to read.
questions.explanation: Of 180.1 billion USDT in circulation, 92.4 billion (51%) is on Tron and 70.9 billion (39%) on Ethereum (31 Oct 2026). Day 3 showed that stablecoins carry most illicit volume, so a stablecoin case will often run through Tron.

questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/permissioned_ledger/01-PC-permissioned_distributed_ledgers.qmd: Half of all USDT sits on Tron

questions.question_stem: A draft assessment says USDT on Tron is "half of supply", copied from a DefiLlama read dated 31 Oct 2026. What should the analyst do before quoting it?
questions.correct_answer: Read the current figure and state it with its date, because supply moves between chains daily.
incorrect_answers: Quote it as it stands, because a share that was true on one date stays true for the whole quarter.
Replace it with Ethereum's share, because a supply share holds steady only on the busiest chain.
Drop the figure, because supply by chain cannot be read from any public source and so cannot be dated.
questions.explanation: Supply by chain moves daily, so the analyst reads the current figure and states it with its date before quoting it.
questions.lesson_block: Half of all USDT sits on Tron
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/permissioned_ledger/01-PC-permissioned_distributed_ledgers.qmd: Half of all USDT sits on Tron

questions.question_stem: A case file holds a USDT address that starts with T and another written as 0x followed by 40 hex characters; the two carry the same 20 bytes. What does the pair suggest?
questions.correct_answer: The first is Tron and the second an EVM chain; one key made both, a lead that one person controls both, to confirm.
incorrect_answers: Both are Ethereum addresses written two ways, so the pair is a finding that one person controls both of them.
The first is Tron and the second Bitcoin, so the same 20 bytes show that one person holds coins on both.
Both are Tron addresses, so the pair is the two accounts that a single Super Representative opened for them.
questions.explanation: A T-address is Tron; a 0x address is an EVM chain, most often Ethereum, so check which. The same 20 bytes mean one key made both, so probably one controller: a lead to confirm with activity or a source before writing it.
questions.lesson_block: Check: T-address, 0x address: which chain?
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/permissioned_ledger/01-PC-permissioned_distributed_ledgers.qmd: Check: T-address, 0x address: which chain?

questions.question_stem: A Transfer log on Tron's USDT contract shows the value 2500000000, and the contract reports 6 decimals. How much USDT moved?
questions.correct_answer: 2,500 USDT, because the raw value is divided by 10 to the 6th for the contract's 6 decimals.
incorrect_answers: 2,500,000,000 USDT, because the value in a Transfer log is already counted in whole units of USDT.
250 USDT, because the raw value is divided by 10 to the 7th once the Energy fee is taken out of it.
25,000,000 USDT, because a contract with 6 decimals counts its values in hundredths of a whole unit.
questions.explanation: The Transfer log carries a raw value. USDT's contract reports 6 decimals, so 2,500,000,000 divided by 10 to the 6th is 2,500 USDT.

questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/permissioned_ledger/01-PC-permissioned_distributed_ledgers.qmd: Worked: a USDT transfer on Tron, field by field

questions.question_stem: A Tron address received 2,500 USDT. It then sent its whole USDT balance to a wallet an exchange publishes as its own, burning 15 TRX that a third account had sent it. What does the analyst write?
questions.correct_answer: Moderate confidence that it is a deposit address at the exchange; name the deposit, and note that the third account paid for the sweep.
incorrect_answers: High confidence that it belongs to a named customer of the exchange, because the sweep shows who holds the deposit address.
Low confidence, because an address that holds no TRX of its own cannot be a deposit address at any exchange, and a sweep proves nothing.
Moderate confidence that the third account owns the deposit address, because it paid for the sweep from its own funds at once.
questions.explanation: A whole balance sent to one destination soon after is a sweep, and the exchange's published list labels the destination, so two lines agree: Moderate, since both come from the same sweep. The exchange, not the chain, knows the account holder, so the analyst names the deposit. The payer is a link, not an owner.
questions.lesson_block: Worked: a deposit, its sweep, who paid Energy
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/permissioned_ledger/01-PC-permissioned_distributed_ledgers.qmd: Worked: a deposit, its sweep, who paid Energy

questions.question_stem: Today's read of isBlackListed for a Tron address returns true. A draft says the address was frozen before the suspect's transfers. What is wrong?
questions.correct_answer: The read gives the status at the block it was made at; the AddedBlackList event gives the block and time of the freeze.
incorrect_answers: Nothing is wrong, since a true read today shows that the freeze was already in place when the transfers were made.
The read gives the full history of the address, and the AddedBlackList event gives only its current status now.
The AddedBlackList event is logged only when a freeze is lifted, so it cannot be used to date the original freeze of the address.
questions.explanation: isBlackListed answers for the block it is read at. The AddedBlackList event gives the block and time, so the analyst sets that against the transfers.
questions.lesson_block: A freeze is true only at the time of the read
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/permissioned_ledger/01-PC-permissioned_distributed_ledgers.qmd: A freeze is true only at the time of the read

questions.question_stem: An address reads as not blacklisted today. Can the analyst say it was never frozen?
questions.correct_answer: No. A later RemovedBlackList undoes a freeze, so the AddedBlackList events must be read for the history.
incorrect_answers: Yes. A freeze cannot be lifted once Tether's owner wallet has added the address to the blacklist of USDT.
Yes. The status read today is the full record of the address, so one that reads false was never added to it.
No. Only the Super Representatives can lift a freeze, so their votes must be read to see the whole history.
questions.explanation: A later RemovedBlackList undoes a freeze, so a status read today may not be the status then. The analyst reads the AddedBlackList and RemovedBlackList events for the history.
questions.lesson_block: A freeze is true only at the time of the read
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/permissioned_ledger/01-PC-permissioned_distributed_ledgers.qmd: A freeze is true only at the time of the read

questions.question_stem: An address received a victim's 2,500 USDT and swept it at 10:32. At 12:30 the USDT contract logged AddedBlackList for it, and today isBlackListed returns true. Did the freeze stop the victim's money?
questions.correct_answer: No. The freeze came after the sweep, so the money had left; the lead is the exchange that holds the records for the deposit.
incorrect_answers: Yes. The status reads true today, so the 2,500 USDT is held at the address until Tether's owner wallet releases it.
Yes. A freeze reaches back to the sweep, so the swept 2,500 USDT is returned to the address that had held it before.
No. A blacklisted address can no longer receive, so the sweep failed and the funds remain with the victim still.
questions.explanation: The sweep at 10:32 moved the whole balance two hours before the freeze, so the address was empty when frozen. A freeze holds only what is still at the address. The lead is the sweep's destination, the exchange.
questions.lesson_block: Check: the freeze came two hours late
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/permissioned_ledger/01-PC-permissioned_distributed_ledgers.qmd: Check: the freeze came two hours late

questions.question_stem: On what does trust rest in a permissioned ledger, where it rested on costly work in Bitcoin and on stake in Ethereum?
questions.correct_answer: Identity and policy: only organizations the operator admits take part, each known by its own certificate.
incorrect_answers: Computing power: the admitted organizations compete to solve a puzzle before each of them may add a block to it.
Staked coins: each admitted organization locks a deposit that is lost if it signs a record the others reject.
Anonymity: the operator hides every member's name so that no organization can be pressed to alter its records.
questions.explanation: In Hyperledger Fabric a membership service provider maps each participant to a certificate from its organization's authority, and an endorsement policy says whose signatures count. The operator admits members and writes the policy.
questions.lesson_block: Permissioned: the operator decides who writes
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/permissioned_ledger/01-PC-permissioned_distributed_ledgers.qmd: Permissioned: the operator decides who writes

questions.question_stem: A T-address sends 40,000 USDT to an address a bank publishes as its way into a tokenized-deposit ledger the bank runs on Fabric, and no more transfers appear on Tron. What can the analyst say?
questions.correct_answer: The transfer, its block and time, and that it reached the bank's address; the bank is the operator, and its ledger holds the next records.
incorrect_answers: Nothing about the funds, because a trace that ends at a permissioned ledger is void and the trail has gone completely cold for good.
Where the funds went next, because the public Tron record keeps following the funds inside the bank's own ledger after they arrive.
Everything, because the bank publishes its ledger on a public explorer as soon as an outside transfer is first received there.
questions.explanation: An outsider sees no node, no explorer and no copy of the ledger. The analyst states everything up to the edge, names the bank as the operator, and does not report that the trail went cold.
questions.lesson_block: Check: funds leave Tron for a bank's ledger
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/permissioned_ledger/01-PC-permissioned_distributed_ledgers.qmd: Check: funds leave Tron for a bank's ledger

questions.question_stem: A foreign central bank runs its CBDC on a ledger it operates. What can a US analyst say about payments on it?
questions.correct_answer: Name the central bank as the operator and gatekeeper; its ledger is permissioned, so the trace stops at its edge.
incorrect_answers: Trace each payment as USDT is traced on Tron, because a CBDC on a ledger is read from a public explorer by anyone.
Name Tether as the gatekeeper, because a CBDC is a stablecoin and the issuer's owner wallet can freeze it.
Name no real operator, because a CBDC is run by its holders and no single organization decides who may read it.
questions.explanation: A CBDC run on a ledger is a permissioned ledger with the central bank as operator, so the central bank decides who can read it. The analyst names the operator; the trace stops at its edge.
questions.lesson_block: A CBDC is a ledger a central bank runs
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/permissioned_ledger/01-PC-permissioned_distributed_ledgers.qmd: A CBDC is a ledger a central bank runs

questions.question_stem: In an instructor's Fabric demo, peers are taken offline and new writes fail. Why?
questions.correct_answer: The endorsement policy names whose peers must sign a write, so with too few of them the write is not valid.
incorrect_answers: The ledger is mined by those peers, so with fewer of them online the puzzle for the next block cannot be solved.
The orderer needs every peer online to read each write, so a missing peer stops the write from being ordered.
Each organization's authority revokes a member's certificate when its peer is offline, so its writes fail.
questions.explanation: The endorsement policy decides whose peers must sign for a write to be valid.
questions.lesson_block: Fabric demo: watch the gatekeeper work
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/permissioned_ledger/01-PC-permissioned_distributed_ledgers.qmd: Fabric demo: watch the gatekeeper work

questions.question_stem: A T-address holds 12,000 USDT that arrived yesterday and has sent nothing since. Who is the gatekeeper, and what can it do?
questions.correct_answer: Tether, through USDT's owner wallet: it can freeze the address, and the balance is still there to hold.
incorrect_answers: No one, because an open ledger has no gatekeeper, so the 12,000 USDT cannot be stopped by anyone at all.
The 27 Super Representatives, who can freeze the address by a vote and who also decide who reads its records.
Tether, but only after the Super Representatives approve the freeze by a vote of at least 19 of the 27 producers.
questions.explanation: USDT's owner can blacklist the address, and because the 12,000 USDT has not moved, a freeze would hold it. The analyst reads everything from outside and dates every freeze answer.
questions.lesson_block: Practice: name the gatekeeper for three records
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/permissioned_ledger/01-PC-permissioned_distributed_ledgers.qmd: Practice: name the gatekeeper for three records

questions.question_stem: A bc1 address received 0.5 BTC an hour ago, in a block with three confirmations. Who can stop that payment, and where does the next gatekeeper appear?
questions.correct_answer: No one on chain can stop it, since there is no issuer or operator; the next gatekeeper is an exchange the coins reach.
incorrect_answers: The issuer, who can freeze the address as Tether does on Tron; the next gatekeeper is the exchange that sells the coins.
The network's operator, who admits the miners and can reverse a payment its policy rejects; no later gatekeeper exists.
No one on chain, so the trace needs no gatekeeper at all; an exchange the coins reach holds no records to name.
questions.explanation: On Bitcoin no issuer or operator can stop a payment, so the answer is no one on chain; everything is readable and no one is named. The first gatekeeper is the exchange the coins reach.
questions.lesson_block: Answers: three gatekeepers, what each can see
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/permissioned_ledger/01-PC-permissioned_distributed_ledgers.qmd: Answers: three gatekeepers, what each can see

questions.question_stem: A sweep on Tron moved USDT from an address that holds no TRX of its own, and a draft note says the sender paid. What should the analyst check?
questions.correct_answer: Which account paid: another account delegated Energy or sent TRX for the sender to burn, and that payer is a link to follow.
incorrect_answers: Nothing, because a USDT transfer on Tron is paid by the sender in TRX as on Ethereum, so the sender always paid it.
Which Super Representative paid, because the producer of a block pays the Energy for every contract call made in it.
Whether the USDT contract paid, because Tether covers the Energy of any transfers from addresses that hold no TRX.
questions.explanation: An address with no TRX can still move USDT: another account delegated Energy, or sent TRX for the sender to burn. That payer's payment is on chain, so it is a link to follow.
questions.lesson_block: Review: every record has a gatekeeper
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/permissioned_ledger/01-PC-permissioned_distributed_ledgers.qmd: Review: every record has a gatekeeper

questions.question_stem: A case follows USDT on Tron, which Tether could still freeze, and the funds later enter a CBDC ledger. How should the analyst state who could stop the money at each point?
questions.correct_answer: On Tron, Tether, by freezing, dated by block; in the CBDC ledger, the central bank as operator, seen only up to its edge.
incorrect_answers: On Tron, the 27 Super Representatives, by vote; in the CBDC ledger, the same group, since both ledgers are run alike.
On Tron, no one, since the chain is open; in the CBDC ledger, Tether, which holds the keys for the central bank.
On Tron, Tether, as read today; in the CBDC ledger, any member, since each can read and stop the other's payments.
questions.explanation: Each ledger has a gatekeeper to name. For USDT the issuer is the gatekeeper and its freeze is dated by block; on a permissioned ledger the operator is, and the trace stops at its edge.
questions.lesson_block: A CBDC is a ledger a central bank runs
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/permissioned_ledger/01-PC-permissioned_distributed_ledgers.qmd: A CBDC is a ledger a central bank runs

questions.question_stem: The Tron resource model, as the lesson quotes it, gives Energy no free quota. How does an account obtain the Energy for a USDT transfer?
questions.correct_answer: It stakes TRX, receives Energy that another account delegated, or burns TRX as a fallback when it has neither.
incorrect_answers: It draws on a free daily Energy quota that Tron resets for every account that holds any USDT at all.
It pays a fee in USDT to the producing Super Representative, who hands the Energy back from the block reward at once.
It borrows Energy from Tether, whose owner wallet pays it for every transfer of the USDT token on Tron.
questions.explanation: The lesson quotes the Tron resource model: an account must stake (or receive delegated) TRX to obtain Energy, or rely on the TRX-burn fallback. A USDT transfer is a contract call, so it uses Energy.
questions.lesson_block: Energy pays for a USDT move: who staked it?
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/permissioned_ledger/01-PC-permissioned_distributed_ledgers.qmd: Energy pays for a USDT move: who staked it?
questions.specific_source_reading: Tron developer documentation, resource model: Energy has no free quota; stake, delegation or TRX burn, as the slide quotes it

questions.question_stem: Tron's consensus has 27 Super Representatives elected by stakers' votes. When is a block solidified, and what should the analyst read?
questions.correct_answer: Once at least 19 distinct Super Representatives have each produced a block at or above it; read solidified data only.
incorrect_answers: Once all 27 Super Representatives have each signed that block; read the newest block, since it is the final one on chain.
Once Tether's owner wallet has approved that block; read any block, since the issuer's approval makes the block final.
Once about 3 seconds have passed since it was made; read any block older than that, since it cannot be changed.
questions.explanation: The Tron consensus documentation, as the lesson states it: 27 Super Representatives make a block about every 3 seconds, and a block is solidified once at least 19 distinct ones have built at or above it. The analyst reads solidified data only.

questions.specific_source_reading: Tron developer documentation, consensus: 27 Super Representatives, solidified once 19 have built on a block, as the slide states it

questions.question_stem: USDT's contract on Tron has addBlackList, removeBlackList and destroyBlackFunds. Who can call them, and what shows a freeze on chain?
questions.correct_answer: Only the contract's owner, a multisignature wallet (5 Nov 2026); a freeze shows as an AddedBlackList event on it.
incorrect_answers: Any of the 27 Super Representatives; a freeze shows as a Transfer log to an address that Tether itself controls.
Any holder, by paying the Energy for the call; a freeze shows as a change in that holder's own TRX balance.
Only the 27 Super Representatives by vote; a freeze shows as a solidified block that holds no transactions of the address.
questions.explanation: The lesson cites the USDT contract on Tron: the same owner-only functions as on Ethereum, with the AddedBlackList event. As of 5 Nov 2026 the owner is a multisignature wallet with three keys, two of which must agree. The Super Representatives make blocks; only the owner can freeze.

questions.question_stem: A Fabric ordering service runs Raft with three ordering nodes, and one of them crashes. Does the ledger keep going?
questions.correct_answer: Yes. Raft keeps going while a majority of ordering nodes stay up, and two of three is a majority.
incorrect_answers: No. Raft keeps going only while every ordering node stays up, so one crash is enough to stop the ledger.
No. Raft keeps going only while the operator's node stays up, so a crash of any other node stops it.
Yes. Raft keeps going while under a third of the ordering nodes lie, and a crashed node counts as one.
questions.explanation: The lesson, citing the Fabric ordering-service documentation: Raft, Fabric's recommended orderer, is crash fault tolerant and keeps going while a majority of ordering nodes stay up. It assumes no node lies.
questions.lesson_block: Permissioned: the operator decides who writes
questions.specific_source_lesson: blockchain-course/lessons/permissioned_ledger/01-PC-permissioned_distributed_ledgers.qmd: Permissioned: the operator decides who writes
questions.specific_source_reading: Fabric documentation, ordering service, and Ongaro and Ousterhout on Raft: crash fault tolerant, a majority must stay up, as the slide states it

questions.question_stem: A permissioned ledger orders its blocks with a BFT protocol of the PBFT kind. When does it keep going, and what may its failed nodes do?
questions.correct_answer: It keeps going while under a third of the nodes lie; a node that has failed may lie, not only crash.
incorrect_answers: It keeps going while a majority of the nodes stay up; its failed nodes may only crash and never lie.
It keeps going while under half of the nodes lie; its failed nodes may lie, not only crash.
It keeps going only while every node tells the truth; one node that lies is enough to stop the ledger.
questions.explanation: The lesson, citing Castro and Liskov and the Fabric documentation: PBFT is Byzantine fault tolerant and keeps going while under a third of the nodes lie. Fabric 3.0 added a BFT orderer of this kind. Raft, by contrast, survives only crashes.

questions.question_stem: A Fabric network's ordering service is run by one bank, but the endorsement policy for transfers needs signatures from two other banks. Can the ordering bank move an asset on its own?
questions.correct_answer: No. The ordering service only packages endorsed transactions into a block; the policy decides whose signatures make a write valid.
incorrect_answers: Yes. Whoever runs the ordering service decides which transactions are valid, so it can approve the transfer on its own.
Yes. The ordering bank's certificate outranks the endorsers' certificates, so its transfer is valid without their signatures.
No. Only the organization's authority can move assets, so the ordering bank must first ask its authority to sign the transfer.
questions.explanation: The lesson, citing Androulaki et al. and the Fabric documentation: the endorsement policy names which organizations' peers must sign before a transaction is valid, and the ordering service orders endorsed transactions and packages them into a block. Running the orderer does not replace the endorsements the policy names.

questions.question_stem: A Fabric channel has a private data collection. What do channel peers outside the collection hold?
questions.correct_answer: Only a hash of the private data, while a defined subset of organizations on the channel holds that data.
incorrect_answers: The full data in an encrypted form, since every peer keeps a copy that only the subset can read.
Nothing at all, since peers outside the collection do not learn that a private transaction was made.
A summary of the data, because the orderer publishes it to the whole channel when it commits each new block.
questions.explanation: The lesson quotes the Fabric private data documentation: a collection lets a defined subset of organizations on a channel read the data, every other peer on the channel gets only a hash, and the orderer does not see the private data.
